title: Leaders Who Devour Their People
overview: Micah confronts the rulers, priests and prophets of Jerusalem who profit from injustice, and warns that their city will fall because of it.

parts.label: Rulers who eat the people (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Micah speaks to the nation's leaders, the very people whose job was to know and uphold justice. The gruesome butcher imagery is a picture: they stripped ordinary people of money, land and livelihood as if carving them up for a cooking pot.

parts.label: Cries that go unanswered (v. 4)
parts.note: When disaster comes, these leaders will call on the LORD and hear nothing back. It mirrors how they ignored the cries of the people they crushed.

parts.label: Prophets for hire (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: Some prophets promised peace to anyone who fed them and declared war in God's name on anyone who did not. Micah says their light will go out, and they will be disgraced and left speechless because they have no real answer from God.

parts.label: Micah's different calling (v. 8)
parts.note: Unlike the paid prophets, Micah says the Spirit of the LORD gives him power, courage and a sense of what is right. His task is to name the nation's wrongs, not to flatter it.

parts.label: Bribes and false security (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: Judges took bribes, priests charged for teaching God's law, prophets sold predictions, and fine buildings went up on money gained through violence and injustice. Yet the leaders felt safe, assuming that because God's temple stood among them, nothing bad could happen.

parts.label: Jerusalem in ruins (v. 12)
parts.note: Micah warns that the city will be plowed like a field and the temple hill left as an overgrown heap. About a century later this warning was recalled (Jeremiah 26:18) as one King Hezekiah had taken to heart, and Babylon later destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC.

think: What makes it hard to tell someone an uncomfortable truth when your income or standing depends on keeping them pleased?
